chapter: Ch 12 — The Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 3 · Nature of an LLP
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a limited liability partnership under section 3 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008?

readLink.label: Read: Nature of an LLP — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: A body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act, which is a legal entity separate from its partners and has perpetual succession
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(1) makes an LLP a body corporate and a separate legal entity; s. 3(2) gives it perpetual succession.

options.text: An association of persons carrying on business in partnership, which is not a separate legal entity
options.explanation: That describes a partnership firm under the Indian Partnership Act 1932. An LLP is expressly a body corporate and a separate legal entity.

options.text: A body corporate that acquires perpetual succession only if the LLP agreement so provides
options.explanation: Perpetual succession is conferred by s. 3(2) itself. The LLP agreement governs mutual rights and duties (s. 23), not the existence of the entity.

options.text: A company registered under the Companies Act 2013 with the liability of its members limited by guarantee
options.explanation: An LLP is incorporated under the LLP Act 2008, not the Companies Act 2013, and it has no share capital and no guarantee clause.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 3(3) · Change in partners
questions.stem: Under section 3(3) of the LLP Act 2008, a change in the partners of an LLP:

readLink.label: Read: Nature of an LLP — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: Dissolves the existing LLP and reconstitutes a new one from the date of the change
options.explanation: That is the position for a partnership firm, which is only a compendious name for the partners. An LLP is a body corporate and survives the change.

options.text: Does not affect the existence, rights or liabilities of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(3) states exactly this, which is the practical content of perpetual succession under s. 3(2).

options.text: Affects the liabilities of the LLP but not its existence
options.explanation: Section 3(3) protects existence, rights AND liabilities. Splitting the three is the standard misreading.

options.text: Requires a fresh certificate of incorporation to be issued by the Registrar
options.explanation: A change in partners is notified under s. 25(2) within 30 days. A fresh certificate of incorporation follows only a change of name (s. 17(3)).

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 2(1)(ta) · Small LLP
questions.stem: As the law stands, a 'small LLP' under section 2(1)(ta) of the LLP Act 2008 is one whose:

readLink.label: Read: Nature of an LLP — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: Paid-up capital does not exceed ₹50 lakh and whose average annual turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore
options.explanation: Those were the One Person Company conversion thresholds under the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, since omitted. An LLP has no paid-up capital at all.

options.text: Contribution does not exceed ₹40 lakh and whose turnover does not exceed ₹25 lakh
options.explanation: The two figures are transposed. The contribution ceiling is the lower one (₹25 lakh) and the turnover ceiling the higher one (₹40 lakh).

options.text: Contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh and whose turnover as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed ₹40 lakh
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs must be satisfied, and the turnover limb is tested on the immediately preceding financial year.

options.text: Contribution does not exceed ₹5 crore and whose turnover does not exceed ₹50 crore
options.explanation: Those are the statutory OUTER limits up to which the Central Government may raise the prescribed ceilings; they are not the operative ceilings.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 2(1)(ta) · Small LLP applied
questions.stem: Shreyas Bhairavi LLP has a total contribution of partners of ₹22,00,000. Its turnover as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year is ₹46,00,000. Applying section 2(1)(ta), the LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: Nature of an LLP — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: A small LLP, because its contribution is within the prescribed ceiling
options.explanation: Satisfying one limb is not enough. Section 2(1)(ta) joins the contribution limb and the turnover limb by 'and'.

options.text: Not a small LLP, because the turnover ceiling of ₹40 lakh is exceeded
options.explanation: Correct. Contribution ₹22 lakh is within ₹25 lakh, but turnover ₹46 lakh exceeds ₹40 lakh, and both limbs must be satisfied.

options.text: Not a small LLP, because the contribution ceiling of ₹25 lakh is exceeded
options.explanation: The contribution of ₹22 lakh is comfortably inside the ₹25 lakh ceiling. It is the turnover limb that fails.

options.text: Not a small LLP, because both the ceilings are exceeded
options.explanation: Only one ceiling is exceeded. Reading both as breached suggests the two figures have been compared with the wrong limits.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 4 · Indian Partnership Act 1932
questions.stem: The relationship between the Indian Partnership Act 1932 and an LLP incorporated under the LLP Act 2008 is that the 1932 Act:

readLink.label: Read: Nature of an LLP — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: Applies to an LLP in all matters on which the LLP Act 2008 is silent
options.explanation: That is what students expect, but s. 4 excludes the 1932 Act outright. Gaps in the mutual rights of partners are filled by the First Schedule under s. 23(4), not by the 1932 Act.

options.text: Applies only to the mutual rights and duties of the partners of an LLP
options.explanation: Mutual rights and duties are governed by the LLP agreement and, where it is silent, by the First Schedule. The 1932 Act has no role.

options.text: Applies to an LLP that was converted from a firm registered under that Act
options.explanation: On conversion the firm is deemed dissolved and removed from the register of firms. What emerges is an LLP governed wholly by the 2008 Act.

options.text: Does not apply to an LLP, save as otherwise provided
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 excludes the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which is why a partner is not the agent of the other partners and their liability is not joint and several.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · LLP compared with a partnership firm
questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct point of distinction between an LLP and a partnership firm?
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, ss. 3, 26 and 28 read against the Indian Partnership Act 1932

readLink.label: Read: LLP compared with a partnership and a company →

options.text: A partner of an LLP is the agent of the LLP but not of the other partners, whereas a partner of a firm is the agent of the firm and also of the other partners
options.explanation: Correct. Section 26 of the LLP Act deliberately drops the mutual-agency limb found in s. 18 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which is why an LLP partner is not liable for another partner's wrongful act.

options.text: An LLP must have a minimum of seven partners, whereas a firm needs only two
options.explanation: Section 6(1) requires only two partners, the same minimum as a firm. Seven is the public-company minimum under the Companies Act 2013.

options.text: A firm has perpetual succession, whereas an LLP is dissolved whenever a partner retires
options.explanation: This reverses the position. Perpetual succession belongs to the LLP under s. 3(2)-(3); a firm changes with its partners.

options.text: An LLP is restricted to a maximum of fifty partners, whereas a firm has no maximum
options.explanation: There is no maximum number of partners for an LLP. The fifty-member limit belongs to associations under the Companies Act rules.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · LLP compared with a company
questions.stem: Which of the following is a genuine difference between an LLP and a company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013?
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, ss. 14, 23 and 34 read against the Companies Act 2013

readLink.label: Read: LLP compared with a partnership and a company →

options.text: A company is a separate legal entity, whereas an LLP is not
options.explanation: Both are bodies corporate and separate legal entities. Section 3(1) of the LLP Act says so in terms.

options.text: A company enjoys perpetual succession, whereas an LLP does not
options.explanation: Section 3(2) confers perpetual succession on an LLP as well.

options.text: The mutual rights and duties of the partners of an LLP are governed by the LLP agreement, whereas a company's internal governance is largely prescribed by the Act, the memorandum and the articles
options.explanation: Correct. This contractual freedom, backed by the First Schedule where the agreement is silent, is the defining structural difference; a company must follow the statutory scheme of meetings, resolutions and board powers.

options.text: An LLP must get its accounts audited every year, whereas a company need do so only above prescribed thresholds
options.explanation: This is exactly reversed. Audit is compulsory for every company, whereas an LLP is audited only above the Rule 24 thresholds.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 5 · Who may be a partner
questions.stem: Under section 5 of the LLP Act 2008, which of the following cannot become a partner of an LLP?

readLink.label: Read: Partners — ss. 5, 6 and 22 →

options.text: A company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013
options.explanation: A body corporate may be a partner, and a company is a body corporate. It will simply have to nominate an individual to act as a designated partner under the proviso to s. 7(1).

options.text: An individual who is a discharged insolvent
options.explanation: Only an UNDISCHARGED insolvent is disqualified. Discharge removes the disability.

options.text: A partnership firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act 1932
options.explanation: Correct. Section 5 admits only an individual or a body corporate, and a firm is neither — it has no separate legal personality. Its partners may join in their individual capacity instead.

options.text: A body corporate incorporated outside India
options.explanation: Section 5 says 'body corporate' without territorial limitation, and s. 2(1)(d) includes an LLP or company incorporated outside India.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 6(2) · Sole partner clock
questions.stem: Anantha Consultants LLP had two partners. On 14 May 2026 one of them retires, leaving Vedika as the only partner, and Vedika knowingly carries on the business. Obligations of the LLP incurred by Vedika become her personal liability under section 6(2) only if they are incurred after:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 6(2) — six months of continued business

readLink.label: Read: Partners — ss. 5, 6 and 22 →

options.text: 14 August 2026
options.explanation: That is three months. Section 6(2) allows more than six months of continued business before personal liability attaches.

options.text: 10 November 2026
options.explanation: That is 180 days counted day by day from 14 May 2026. Section 6(2) speaks of six MONTHS, so the calendar-month count applies.

options.text: 14 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Six calendar months from 14 May 2026. Obligations incurred after this date, while Vedika is the only partner and knows it, are her personal liability.
That is twelve months. No twelve-month grace exists under s. 6(2).

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 6(2) · Ingredients of personal liability
questions.stem: Section 6(2) of the LLP Act 2008 fastens personal liability on a sole surviving partner. That liability arises only where:

readLink.label: Read: Partners — ss. 5, 6 and 22 →

options.text: The number of partners falls below two, whatever the sole partner knew and whatever the LLP did afterwards
options.explanation: Falling below two is only the first ingredient. Continued business beyond six months and the sole partner's knowledge are both required.

options.text: The LLP carries on business with one partner for any period, and that partner is then liable for all the obligations of the LLP from its incorporation
options.explanation: Two errors. There is a six-month grace, and liability reaches only the obligations incurred during the period of continued short-handed business.

options.text: The Tribunal has first ordered the LLP to be wound up under section 64(b)
options.explanation: Section 6(2) operates on its own. Being below two partners for more than six months is separately a GROUND for winding up under s. 64(b), but no order is a precondition.

options.text: The LLP carries on business for more than six months while reduced below two partners, and the sole partner has knowledge of that fact — and then only for obligations incurred during that continued period
options.explanation: Correct. Three ingredients: the six-month period expires, business continues, and the sole partner knows. Liability is confined to obligations incurred in that continued period.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 7(1) · Minimum designated partners
questions.stem: Section 7(1) of the LLP Act 2008 requires every LLP to have:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: At least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom shall be a resident in India
options.explanation: Correct. Both requirements are cumulative: two designated partners, both individuals, and at least one of them resident in India.

options.text: At least two designated partners, who may be individuals or bodies corporate
options.explanation: A designated partner must be an individual. Where the partners are bodies corporate, individual NOMINEES of those bodies act as designated partners.

options.text: At least one designated partner, who shall be a resident in India
options.explanation: One is not enough. If at any time there is only one designated partner, the proviso to s. 9 deems every partner to be a designated partner.

options.text: At least three designated partners, of whom two shall be residents in India
options.explanation: There is no three-designated-partner requirement anywhere in the Act.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 7 Explanation · Residence test
questions.stem: Mr Rangan is the only individual designated partner of Meghdoot Infratech LLP who spends any time in India. During the financial year 2026-27 he stayed in India for 96 days. To make him a 'resident in India' for the purposes of section 7(1) for that financial year, the number of ADDITIONAL days he must stay in India during that same financial year is:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 7 Explanation (as amended in 2021) — 120 days in the financial year

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: 24 days
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 7 requires a stay of not less than 120 days during the financial year; 120 less 96 already spent leaves 24.

options.text: 86 days
options.explanation: That applies the pre-2021 test of 182 days. The 2021 Amendment reduced the requirement to 120 days and changed the reference period to the financial year.

options.text: 84 days
options.explanation: That assumes a 180-day test, which appears nowhere in the LLP Act.

options.text: Nil — he is already a resident in India
options.explanation: 96 days falls short of the 120-day threshold, so he is not yet a resident for this purpose.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 7(4), 7(5) and 7(6) · Consent, filing and DPIN
questions.stem: Which set of requirements must be satisfied before and after an individual becomes a designated partner of an LLP?

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: He must be a partner of the LLP for at least one year, and must then be appointed by a resolution of all the partners
options.explanation: No qualifying period exists, and appointment follows the incorporation document or the LLP agreement, not a prescribed resolution.

options.text: He must give his prior consent to act in the prescribed form, the LLP must file his particulars with the Registrar within 30 days of his appointment, and he must obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number
options.explanation: Correct. Section 7(4) requires prior consent, s. 7(5) requires the particulars to be filed within 30 days of appointment, and s. 7(6) requires a DPIN, with ss. 153 to 159 of the Companies Act 2013 applying mutatis mutandis.

options.text: He must obtain a Director Identification Number under the Companies Act 2013 and be a director of at least one company
options.explanation: He needs a DPIN, and although the DIN and DPIN systems are unified in practice, directorship of a company is nowhere required.

options.text: His consent may be given at any time within 30 days after he begins to act, provided it is filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: The consent under s. 7(4) must be PRIOR. Only the filing of particulars enjoys the 30-day window.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 8 · Liabilities of designated partners
questions.stem: Unless expressly provided otherwise in the Act, a designated partner of an LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: Liable for all the debts of the LLP without limit, in addition to his contribution
options.explanation: Section 8 imposes compliance responsibility and penalty liability, not liability for the LLP's trade debts. Unlimited liability arises only under s. 30 for fraud.

options.text: Responsible only for the filings expressly listed in the LLP agreement
options.explanation: The LLP agreement may add duties, but the statutory responsibility for compliance with the Act, including every document, return and statement, exists independently of it.

options.text: Responsible for doing all acts, matters and things required to be done by the LLP for compliance with the Act, including filing every document, return and statement, and liable to all penalties imposed on the LLP for contravention of those provisions
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the two limbs of s. 8 — compliance responsibility and exposure to the penalties imposed on the LLP.

options.text: Liable to penalties only where he has personally signed the defaulting document
options.explanation: Section 8 attaches to the office, not to the signature. Every designated partner is exposed unless the Act expressly provides otherwise.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 9 · Filling a vacancy
questions.stem: A vacancy in the office of designated partner of Girikandra Foods LLP arises on 22 June 2026. Under section 9, the LLP may appoint a designated partner in that vacancy at the latest by:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 9 — 30 days from the vacancy

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: 7 July 2026
options.explanation: That is 15 days. Fifteen days is the period in s. 25(1) for a partner to inform the LLP of a change in his own name or address, not the s. 9 period.

options.text: 22 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9 allows 30 days from the date the vacancy arises, counted from 22 June 2026.

options.text: 21 August 2026
options.explanation: That is 60 days. Sixty days is the annual-return period in s. 35 and the appeal period under s. 68A, not the s. 9 period.

options.text: 22 September 2026
options.explanation: That is three months, which is the s. 17(1) period for complying with a name direction.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · Proviso to s. 9 · Deemed designated partners
questions.stem: Where an LLP fails to appoint a designated partner, or where at any time there is only one designated partner, the consequence under the proviso to section 9 is that:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners — ss. 7 to 10 →

options.text: The LLP stands dissolved and the Registrar strikes its name off the register
options.explanation: Nothing of the sort follows. Strike off under s. 75 requires the Registrar's reasonable belief that the LLP is not carrying on business, plus a hearing.

options.text: The Registrar appoints a designated partner on behalf of the LLP
options.explanation: The Registrar has no such power. The Act solves the gap by deeming, not by appointing.

options.text: The senior-most partner by age is deemed to be the second designated partner
options.explanation: No seniority rule appears anywhere in the Act.

options.text: Each partner of the LLP is deemed to be a designated partner
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 9 sweeps every partner — including a body corporate partner — into the office, with the compliance responsibility and penalty exposure of s. 8.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 11(1) · Statement of compliance
questions.stem: The statement filed along with the incorporation document, that all the requirements of the LLP Act and the rules in respect of incorporation have been complied with, must be made by:

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation — ss. 11, 12 and 14 →

options.text: An advocate, a Chartered Accountant, a Cost Accountant or a Company Secretary who is engaged in the formation of the LLP, and by anyone who subscribed his name to the incorporation document
options.explanation: Correct. Section 11(1)(c) requires two signatures — a qualified professional ENGAGED IN THE FORMATION, and a subscriber to the incorporation document.

options.text: An advocate alone
options.explanation: An advocate is one of four eligible professionals, and in any event a subscriber's statement is also required.

options.text: Any practising Chartered Accountant, whether or not engaged in the formation of the LLP
options.explanation: The professional must be engaged in the formation of the LLP. A detached certifier will not do.

options.text: All the proposed designated partners, jointly
options.explanation: The Act asks for a professional and a subscriber. Designated partners as such have no role in the s. 11(1)(c) statement.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 12 · Certificate of incorporation
questions.stem: The certificate issued by the Registrar under section 12 of the LLP Act 2008 is:

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation — ss. 11, 12 and 14 →

options.text: Prima facie evidence of incorporation, rebuttable by any interested person within one year
options.explanation: Section 12 uses the stronger formula. There is no one-year rebuttal window.

options.text: Evidence only that the incorporation document was filed, and not that the LLP exists
options.explanation: The certificate certifies that the LLP IS incorporated by the name specified in it.

options.text: Conclusive evidence that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified in it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 12(3) makes the certificate conclusive evidence, which is why the Registrar may accept the s. 11(1)(c) statement as sufficient evidence of compliance.

options.text: Conclusive evidence that every requirement of the Act and the rules has in fact been complied with, so that no person can afterwards be prosecuted for a false statement
options.explanation: The certificate proves incorporation, not innocence. A knowingly false statement under s. 11(1)(c) is punishable under s. 11(3) with imprisonment up to two years and fine.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 14 · Effect of registration
questions.stem: Section 14 of the LLP Act 2008 sets out what an LLP is capable of doing by its name on registration. Which of the following is NOT among them?

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation — ss. 11, 12 and 14 →

options.text: Suing and being sued
options.explanation: Expressly conferred by s. 14(a).

options.text: Acquiring, owning, holding and developing or disposing of property, whether movable or immovable, tangible or intangible
options.explanation: Expressly conferred by s. 14(b).

options.text: Having a common seal, if it decides to have one
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 14(c). Note that the seal is optional, not mandatory.

options.text: Issuing shares and debentures to the public to raise capital
options.explanation: Correct. This is NOT among the capabilities in s. 14. An LLP has no share capital; partners bring 'contribution' under s. 32, and there is no mechanism for a public issue of shares or debentures.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 15 · Name of an LLP
questions.stem: Under section 15(2) of the LLP Act 2008, an LLP shall not be registered by a name which, in the opinion of the Central Government, is undesirable or is identical with or too nearly resembles:

readLink.label: Read: Registered office and the name of an LLP →

options.text: The name of any other LLP only
options.explanation: Far too narrow. The comparison set in s. 15(2)(b) is deliberately wide.

options.text: The name of any other partnership firm, LLP or body corporate, or a registered trade mark, or a trade mark that is the subject matter of a pending application for registration
options.explanation: Correct. Section 15(2)(b) reaches firms and pending trade-mark applications as well, which is wider than the corresponding test for company names.

options.text: The name of any other body corporate or a registered trade mark, but not that of a partnership firm
options.explanation: Partnership firms are expressly included in the s. 15(2)(b) comparison set.

options.text: A registered trade mark only, and then only if the proprietor objects within three years
options.explanation: That confuses s. 15(2) with the separate three-year limit for a trade-mark proprietor's rectification application under the proviso to s. 17(1).

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 17(1) · Rectification of name
questions.stem: On 11 August 2026 the Central Government directs Vasundhara Analytics LLP, on the application of a registered trade-mark proprietor, to change its name under section 17(1). The LLP must change its name at the latest by:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 17(1) — three months from the direction

readLink.label: Read: Registered office and the name of an LLP →

options.text: 26 August 2026
options.explanation: That is 15 days, which is the period in s. 17(2) for giving NOTICE of the change to the Registrar once the change has been made.

options.text: 10 October 2026
options.explanation: That is 60 days, which appears in s. 35 (annual return) and s. 68A (appeal), not in s. 17.

options.text: 11 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 17(1) allows three months from the date of issue of the direction, counted from 11 August 2026.

options.text: 11 February 2027
options.explanation: That is six months. No six-month period appears in s. 17.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 17(3) · Default in changing the name
questions.stem: Where an LLP defaults in complying with a direction of the Central Government to change its name under section 17(1), the consequence is that:

readLink.label: Read: Registered office and the name of an LLP →

options.text: The Registrar strikes the name of the LLP off the register
options.explanation: Strike off under s. 75 has its own trigger — the Registrar's reasonable belief that the LLP is not carrying on business — and is not a sanction for a name default.

options.text: The LLP and its designated partners are punishable with imprisonment
options.explanation: The pre-2021 section carried a fine, and the substituted section carries no imprisonment at all for this default.

options.text: The Tribunal may order the LLP to be wound up on the just and equitable ground
options.explanation: Section 64(f) exists, but s. 17(3) supplies its own specific and automatic consequence rather than sending anybody to the Tribunal.

options.text: The Central Government allots a new name to the LLP, the Registrar enters it in place of the old name and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation with the new name, which the LLP must thereafter use
options.explanation: Correct. That is s. 17(3) as substituted in 2021. The proviso still lets the LLP change that allotted name later under s. 16.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 23(3) · Pre-incorporation agreement
questions.stem: An agreement in writing made before the incorporation of an LLP, between the persons who subscribe their names to the incorporation document, may impose obligations on the LLP:

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule — s. 23 →

options.text: Automatically from the date of incorporation, without anything further
options.explanation: Section 23(3) attaches a condition. Without it the LLP, not being in existence when the agreement was made, is not bound.

options.text: Provided the agreement is ratified by all the partners after the incorporation of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Section 23(3) requires ratification by ALL the partners after incorporation — a statutory solution to the pre-incorporation contract problem that companies do not enjoy.

options.text: Provided the agreement is ratified by a majority in number of the partners after incorporation
options.explanation: A bare majority will not do; s. 23(3) requires all the partners.

options.text: Only if the obligation is also recorded in the incorporation document filed under section 11
options.explanation: The incorporation document carries the name, business, registered office and particulars of partners. It is not the vehicle for ratifying pre-incorporation obligations.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · First Schedule · Sharing of profits
questions.stem: Three partners of an LLP contribute ₹15 lakh, ₹9 lakh and ₹1 lakh respectively. The LLP agreement is silent on the sharing of profits. Profits for the year are ₹75 lakh. They will be shared:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 23(4) with the First Schedule, para 1

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule — s. 23 →

options.text: Equally — ₹25 lakh each
options.explanation: Correct. Where the agreement is silent, para 1 of the First Schedule applies under s. 23(4), and all the partners share EQUALLY in the capital, profits and losses, whatever they contributed.

options.text: In the ratio of contribution — 15 : 9 : 1
options.explanation: There is no proportionate default. The First Schedule chooses equality precisely because contribution ratios are often not meant to fix profit shares.

options.text: In such ratio as the designated partners may determine
options.explanation: Designated partners are the compliance office-holders. They have no power to fix profit shares.

options.text: Not at all, because an LLP agreement silent on profit sharing is void for uncertainty
options.explanation: Silence is exactly what s. 23(4) and the First Schedule exist to cure. Nothing becomes void.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · First Schedule · Decision making
questions.stem: Where the LLP agreement is silent, which of the following may be decided by a resolution passed by a majority in number of the partners, each partner having one vote?
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, First Schedule, paras 6, 7 and 8

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule — s. 23 →

options.text: The introduction of a new person as a partner of the LLP
options.explanation: No person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of ALL the existing partners.

options.text: A change in the nature of the business of the LLP
options.explanation: The proviso to the majority rule requires the consent of ALL the partners for a change in the nature of the business.

options.text: Any other matter or issue relating to the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. The First Schedule makes ordinary matters decidable by a majority in number of the partners, one vote each — subject to the two unanimity carve-outs for admitting a partner and changing the nature of the business.

options.text: The expulsion of a partner from the LLP
options.explanation: No majority of partners can expel a partner unless a power to do so has been conferred by express agreement between the partners.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 24(1) · Notice of resignation
questions.stem: Kalindi Retail LLP has an LLP agreement that says nothing about how a partner may resign. On 9 September 2026 Ravi gives the other partners written notice of his intention to resign, stating no date. Applying section 24(1), Ravi ceases to be a partner on:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 24(1) — 30 days notice where the agreement is silent

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and registration of changes — ss. 24 and 25 →

options.text: 24 September 2026
options.explanation: That is 15 days. Section 24(1) requires a notice of not less than 30 days where the agreement is silent.

options.text: 9 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(1) requires notice in writing of not less than 30 days to the other partners, counted from 9 September 2026.

options.text: 8 November 2026
options.explanation: That is 60 days, which is not the s. 24(1) period.

options.text: 9 December 2026
options.explanation: That is three months, which belongs to s. 17(1).

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 24(3) · The former partner and third parties
questions.stem: A person who has ceased to be a partner of an LLP continues, in relation to a person dealing with the LLP, to be regarded as a partner unless:

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and registration of changes — ss. 24 and 25 →

options.text: He has published a notice of his cessation in a newspaper circulating in the district
options.explanation: Newspaper publication is the public-notice mechanism of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which s. 4 excludes.

options.text: The LLP agreement has been amended to remove his name
options.explanation: An internal amendment is invisible to outsiders and does nothing under s. 24(3).

options.text: He has settled his accounts with the LLP and received his contribution back under section 24(5)
options.explanation: Payment of his dues is a matter between him and the LLP. It has no effect on how a dealing third party may treat him.

options.text: That person has notice that he has ceased to be a partner, or notice of the cessation has been delivered to the Registrar
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(3) gives two alternative escapes: actual notice to the person dealing with the LLP, or delivery of the notice to the Registrar, which protects the former partner against the world.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 25(2)(a) · Filing a change in partners
questions.stem: Ishaan is admitted as a partner of Kalindi Retail LLP on 3 December 2026. The LLP must file notice of the change with the Registrar at the latest by:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 25(2)(a) — 30 days from the change

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and registration of changes — ss. 24 and 25 →

options.text: 18 December 2026
options.explanation: That is 15 days, which is the s. 25(1) period for a PARTNER to inform the LLP of a change in his own name or address.

options.text: 1 February 2027
options.explanation: That is 60 days. Sixty days is the s. 35 annual-return period, not the s. 25(2) period.

options.text: 2 January 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25(2)(a) allows 30 days from the date a person becomes or ceases to be a partner, counted from 3 December 2026.

options.text: 3 March 2027
options.explanation: That is three months, which belongs to s. 17(1).

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 26 · Partner as agent
questions.stem: For the purpose of the business of the LLP, every partner of an LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability — ss. 26 to 31 →

options.text: The agent of the LLP, but not of the other partners
options.explanation: Correct. Section 26 confers agency for the LLP alone. This is the structural reason why one partner cannot make another personally liable.

options.text: The agent of the LLP and of the other partners
options.explanation: That is the position under s. 18 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which s. 4 of the LLP Act excludes.

options.text: The agent of the other partners, but not of the LLP
options.explanation: Exactly the reverse of s. 26.

options.text: An agent of the LLP only where the LLP agreement expressly says so
options.explanation: Agency under s. 26 is statutory. The LLP agreement may restrict a partner's AUTHORITY, which matters under s. 27(1), but it does not create the agency.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 27(1) · When the LLP is not bound
questions.stem: An LLP is NOT bound by anything done by a partner in dealing with a third person where:

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability — ss. 26 to 31 →

options.text: The partner in fact had no authority to act for the LLP in doing that act
options.explanation: Absence of authority alone is not enough. Section 27(1) has a second limb about the third person's state of mind.

options.text: The partner in fact had no authority to act for the LLP in doing that act, AND the third person knew that he had no authority or did not know or believe him to be a partner of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs of s. 27(1) must be satisfied. An outsider who reasonably believed he was dealing with a partner of the LLP binds it despite an internal authority limit.

options.text: The act was outside the objects stated in the incorporation document, whatever the third person knew
options.explanation: An LLP has no objects clause operating as a limit on capacity, and the doctrine of ultra vires does not apply to it in that form.

options.text: The third person did not verify the LLP agreement filed with the Registrar under section 23(2)
options.explanation: There is no constructive-notice duty of that kind here. The test is what the third person actually knew or believed.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 28 · A partner's own wrongful act
questions.stem: Partner Anil of a four-partner LLP signs a negligent professional certificate in the course of the LLP's business, causing loss to a client. The correct position is that:

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability — ss. 26 to 31 →

options.text: Only the LLP is liable; Anil enjoys complete personal immunity under section 28(1)
options.explanation: Section 28(1) shields a partner from liability arising SOLELY by reason of being a partner. Section 28(2) expressly preserves liability for his own wrongful act.

options.text: Only Anil is liable; the LLP is not, because he acted without express authority
options.explanation: Section 27(2) makes the LLP liable where a partner is liable as a result of a wrongful act or omission in the course of the business of the LLP.

options.text: Anil is personally liable for his own wrongful act and the LLP is also liable, but the other three partners are not personally liable
options.explanation: Correct. Section 28(2) fixes Anil, s. 27(2) fixes the LLP, and the second limb of s. 28(2) protects the other partners from liability for another partner's wrongful act.

options.text: All four partners are jointly and severally liable, as in a partnership firm
options.explanation: Joint and several liability of partners belongs to s. 25 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which s. 4 of the LLP Act excludes.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 30 · Unlimited liability in case of fraud
questions.stem: Where an act is carried out by a partner of an LLP with intent to defraud the creditors of the LLP, section 30(1) provides that:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 30(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability — ss. 26 to 31 →

options.text: The liability of every partner of the LLP becomes unlimited, whether or not he participated
options.explanation: Only the LLP and the partners who acted with the fraudulent intent lose the shield. Innocent partners keep their s. 28(1) protection.

options.text: The LLP alone becomes liable without limit, the partners retaining their shield in every case
options.explanation: The partners who acted with intent to defraud are expressly stripped of limited liability by s. 30(1).

options.text: The Tribunal must first declare the act fraudulent before any liability can attach
options.explanation: Section 30(1) operates on proof of the fraudulent intent in the proceeding itself. No prior declaration by the Tribunal is a precondition.

options.text: The liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted with that intent is unlimited, and the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner unless it establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(1) with its proviso — unlimited liability for the fraudulent actors, and a defence for the LLP that reverses the burden onto it.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 32 and 33 · Contribution
questions.stem: Regarding a partner's contribution to an LLP, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Contributions — ss. 32 and 33 →

options.text: It may consist of money, tangible or intangible property, promissory notes and contracts for services performed or to be performed, and its monetary value must be accounted for and disclosed in the accounts of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Section 32(1) lists the permitted forms, and s. 32(2) requires the monetary value of each partner's contribution to be accounted for and disclosed as prescribed.

options.text: It must be in money, since the accounts of an LLP have to disclose a monetary figure
options.explanation: The disclosure requirement is satisfied by valuing a non-cash contribution. It does not confine contribution to cash.

options.text: There is a statutory minimum contribution of ₹1,00,000 for every LLP
options.explanation: No minimum contribution exists. That is one of the ways an LLP differs from a company with share capital.

options.text: A creditor who lent to the LLP relying on a contribution obligation recorded in the LLP agreement is bound by any later compromise between the partners reducing that obligation
options.explanation: Section 33(2) says the opposite: a creditor who acted in reliance on the recorded obligation, without notice of the compromise, may enforce the ORIGINAL obligation.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 34(1) · Books of account
questions.stem: Which statement about the books of account of an LLP is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Books, audit and annual filings — ss. 34, 34A and 35 →

options.text: They must be kept on the accrual basis only, according to the double entry system, at the registered office
options.explanation: The accrual-only requirement belongs to s. 128(1) of the Companies Act 2013. Section 34(1) of the LLP Act permits either basis.

options.text: They may be kept on a cash basis or an accrual basis, must follow the double entry system, and must be maintained at the registered office
options.explanation: Correct. Section 34(1) makes the BASIS optional but the double entry system and the registered-office location mandatory.

options.text: They may be kept on any basis and by any system, at any place the designated partners choose
options.explanation: Both the double entry system and the registered-office location are statutory requirements, not choices.

options.text: They must be kept at the registered office and preserved for three years from the date on which they are made
options.explanation: The location is right but the period is wrong: Rule 24 requires preservation for eight years from the date the books are made.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 34(3) with Rule 24 · Form 8 due date
questions.stem: Suryodaya Handlooms LLP has a financial year ending 31 March 2027. The last date for filing its Statement of Account and Solvency (Form 8) for that financial year with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 34(3) with Rule 24 — 30 days from the end of six months of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: Books, audit and annual filings — ss. 34, 34A and 35 →

options.explanation: That is the annual-return date under s. 35 — 60 days from the close of the financial year. The Statement of Account and Solvency runs on a different clock.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: That is the end of the six months from the close of the financial year. The rule allows a further 30 days after that point.

options.text: 31 October 2027
options.explanation: An off-by-one slip. Six months from 31 March 2027 ends on 30 September 2027 (September has 30 days), and 30 days from there is 30 October, not 31 October.

options.text: 30 October 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Six months from the end of the financial year takes you to 30 September 2027; Rule 24 then allows 30 days, giving 30 October 2027.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 42 · Partner's transferable interest
questions.stem: A partner of an LLP assigns his entire right to a share of the profits and to receive distributions to an outsider. The correct consequence under section 42 is that:

readLink.label: Read: Assignment, investigation and compounding →

options.text: The assignee receives the economic rights assigned, but is not thereby entitled to participate in the management or conduct of the activities of the LLP or to access information about its transactions, and the assignor remains a partner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 42(1) permits the transfer, s. 42(2) preserves the assignor's position and the LLP's existence, and s. 42(3) withholds management and information rights from the assignee.

options.text: The assignee becomes a partner of the LLP in place of the assignor with full management rights
options.explanation: Only economic rights travel. Admission as a partner is governed by s. 22 and the LLP agreement, and, where that is silent, requires the consent of all the partners.

options.text: The assignment causes the disassociation of the assignor and the dissolution and winding up of the LLP
options.explanation: Section 42(2) expressly says the transfer does not by itself cause either consequence.

options.text: The assignment is void, because the rights of a partner in an LLP are not transferable
options.explanation: Section 42(1) makes those rights transferable, wholly or in part.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · Third and Fourth Schedules · Conversion by a company
questions.stem: A private company wishes to convert itself into an LLP. Which condition must it satisfy that a partnership firm converting into an LLP need NOT satisfy?
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, ss. 56 and 57 with the Third and Fourth Schedules

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP — the three Schedules →

options.text: That all its members become partners of the LLP and no one else does
options.explanation: That condition applies to both routes — the Second Schedule requires all the partners of the firm and no one else, and the Third Schedule requires all the shareholders and no one else.

options.text: That there is no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of the application
options.explanation: Correct. The no-security-interest condition appears in the Third and Fourth Schedules, which govern company conversions. It is nowhere in the Second Schedule.

options.text: That it has filed all its returns and accounts up to date
options.explanation: Up-to-date filing is a practical requirement of the conversion forms, not a Schedule condition that distinguishes the two routes.

options.text: That the LLP will carry on the same business as the converting entity
options.explanation: No Schedule imposes a same-business condition on either route.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · s. 64 · Winding up by the Tribunal
questions.stem: Which of the following is a ground on which an LLP may be wound up by the Tribunal under section 64?

readLink.label: Read: Foreign LLPs, compromise, winding up and strike off →

options.text: The number of partners of the LLP has been reduced below two at any time during the financial year
options.explanation: The ground requires the reduction to have subsisted for a period of MORE THAN SIX MONTHS. A momentary shortfall is not a ground.

options.text: The LLP has failed to file its Statement of Account and Solvency or annual return for any two consecutive financial years
options.explanation: The correct period is FIVE consecutive financial years. Two years is the corresponding director-disqualification trigger under the Companies Act 2013.

options.text: The LLP has made default in filing with the Registrar the Statement of Account and Solvency or the annual return for any five consecutive financial years
options.explanation: Correct. This is s. 64(e), and it sits alongside the LLP's own decision, the reduction below two partners for more than six months, acts against the sovereignty and integrity of India, and the just-and-equitable ground.

options.text: The LLP has changed the nature of its business without the consent of all its partners
options.explanation: That is a breach of the First Schedule default rule where the agreement is silent. It gives the partners a remedy between themselves; it is not a s. 64 ground.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 3, 4 and 2(1)(ta) · Nature of an LLP
questions.stem: Explain the nature of a limited liability partnership under the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008, bring out three points of distinction between an LLP and a partnership firm, and state when an LLP is a 'small LLP'. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 3: an LLP is a body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act and is a legal entity separate from its partners; it has perpetual succession; and any change in the partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities

Section 4: the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 do not apply to an LLP, save as otherwise provided; an LLP may be formed by two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit

Three distinctions from a partnership firm: (i) an LLP is a separate legal entity with perpetual succession, a firm is not; (ii) a partner of an LLP is the agent of the LLP but not of the other partners, whereas a partner of a firm is the agent of the firm and of the other partners; (iii) the liability of a partner of an LLP is limited to his contribution, whereas partners of a firm are liable jointly and severally without limit
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, ss. 3, 26 and 28, read against the Indian Partnership Act 1932, ss. 18 and 25

skeleton.point: Small LLP under s. 2(1)(ta): contribution not exceeding ₹25 lakh (or such higher prescribed amount, not exceeding ₹5 crore) AND turnover as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year not exceeding ₹40 lakh (or such higher prescribed amount, not exceeding ₹50 crore); both limbs must be satisfied
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 2(1)(ta) (inserted by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021)

skeleton.point: Points to note: the LLP owns property, sues and is sued in its own name (s. 14); a small LLP enjoys lower fees and a reduced penalty regime but is otherwise fully governed by the Act; the ceilings are expressly raisable by prescription
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 14; ICAI SM P2 Ch 12 — analysis of the small-LLP concession

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 7 to 10 · Designated partners
questions.stem: State who must be appointed as designated partners of an LLP, the conditions to be satisfied before and after their appointment, their liabilities, and the consequences of a vacancy remaining unfilled. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 7(1): every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals, and at least one of them shall be a resident in India; where all the partners are bodies corporate, or where they are a mixture of individuals and bodies corporate, at least two individuals who are partners or nominees of those bodies corporate shall act as designated partners
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 7(1) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Explanation to s. 7: 'resident in India' means a person who has stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year — the amended test, replacing the earlier 182 days during the immediately preceding one year
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, Explanation to s. 7 (as amended by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021)

skeleton.point: Conditions: prior consent to act, given to the LLP in the prescribed form and manner (s. 7(4)); particulars of every individual who has given consent to be filed with the Registrar within 30 days of his appointment (s. 7(5)); every designated partner to obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number, ss. 153 to 159 of the Companies Act 2013 applying mutatis mutandis (s. 7(6))

Section 8: unless expressly provided otherwise, a designated partner is responsible for doing all acts, matters and things required to be done by the LLP in respect of compliance with the Act, including filing every document, return and statement, and such other things as are specified in the LLP agreement, and is liable to all penalties imposed on the LLP for contravention of those provisions

Section 9: a vacancy may be filled within 30 days of its arising, with the s. 7(4) and 7(5) requirements applying; if no designated partner is appointed, or if at any time there is only one, each partner is deemed to be a designated partner; contravention of ss. 7, 8 or 9 attracts a penalty on the LLP and its partners or designated partners under s. 10, adjudicated by the Registrar under s. 68A

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 11 to 17 · Incorporation and name
questions.stem: Describe the process by which an LLP is incorporated, the effect of its registration, and the statutory requirements governing its name, including the consequences of registration with an objectionable name. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 11(1) and (2): two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit subscribe their names to an incorporation document, filed with the Registrar of the State in which the registered office is to be situated; the document states the name, the proposed business, the address of the registered office, and the names and addresses of the persons who are to be partners and designated partners; it is accompanied by a statement of compliance made by an advocate, Chartered Accountant, Cost Accountant or Company Secretary engaged in the formation AND by a subscriber to the incorporation document

Section 11(3): a person who makes that statement knowing it to be false, or not believing it to be true, is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and with fine of not less than ₹10,000 and up to ₹5,00,000

Section 12: the Registrar registers the incorporation document and issues a certificate that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified; he may accept the statement of compliance as sufficient evidence of compliance; the certificate is signed by the Registrar, authenticated by his official seal, and is conclusive evidence that the LLP is incorporated by that name

Section 14: on registration the LLP is, by its name, capable of suing and being sued; of acquiring, owning, holding and developing or disposing of property, movable or immovable, tangible or intangible; of having a common seal if it decides to have one; and of doing and suffering such other acts and things as bodies corporate may lawfully do and suffer

Section 15: every LLP must have the words 'limited liability partnership' or the acronym 'LLP' as the last words of its name; no LLP may be registered by a name that in the opinion of the Central Government is undesirable, or is identical with or too nearly resembles that of any other partnership firm, LLP or body corporate, a registered trade mark, or a trade mark that is the subject matter of a pending application; a name may be reserved under s. 16 for three months from the date of intimation by the Registrar

Section 17: where an LLP is registered with a name identical with or too nearly resembling that of another LLP or company, or a registered trade mark likely to be mistaken for it, the Central Government may on application direct a change within three months of the direction (a trade-mark proprietor applying within three years of incorporation, registration or change of name); notice of the change to be given to the Registrar within 15 days, and the LLP agreement changed within 30 days of the change in the certificate; on default the Central Government allots a new name and the Registrar issues a fresh certificate of incorporation
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 17 (as substituted by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021)

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 26 to 30 · Extent of liability
questions.stem: Explain the extent of the liability of an LLP and of its partners under the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008, including the position where a partner acts without authority, where he commits a wrongful act, where a person holds himself out as a partner, and where an act is done with intent to defraud creditors. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 26: every partner of an LLP is, for the purpose of the business of the LLP, the agent of the LLP, but not of the other partners — in contrast with s. 18 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932

Section 27(1): the LLP is not bound by anything done by a partner in dealing with a person if (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP in doing that particular act, AND (b) the person knows that he has no authority, or does not know or believe him to be a partner of the LLP; both limbs must be satisfied

Sections 27(2) to (4) and 28: the LLP is liable where a partner is liable to any person as a result of a wrongful act or omission on his part in the course of the business of the LLP or with its authority; an obligation of the LLP, whether in contract or otherwise, is solely the obligation of the LLP and is met out of its property; a partner is not personally liable merely by reason of being a partner, but remains personally liable for his OWN wrongful act or omission and is not liable for that of any other partner

Section 29: a person who represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, to be a partner is liable to anyone who on the faith of that representation gives credit to the LLP; and where the LLP receives credit as a result, the LLP is liable to the extent of the credit received or the financial benefit derived, without prejudice to that person's liability; the continued use of a deceased partner's name does not by itself make his legal representative or estate liable for acts done after his death

Section 30: where an act is carried out by the LLP or any of its partners with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who so acted is unlimited for all or any of the debts and liabilities of the LLP; where the act is that of a partner, the LLP is liable to the same extent unless it establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority; compensation is payable to persons who suffer loss from affairs conducted in a fraudulent manner

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 55 to 58 and the Schedules · Conversion into an LLP
questions.stem: State which entities may convert themselves into an LLP, the conditions each must satisfy, the effect of registration of the conversion, and the obligations of the LLP after conversion. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Three routes: a firm may convert under s. 55 in accordance with the Second Schedule; a private company under s. 56 in accordance with the Third Schedule; and an unlisted public company under s. 57 in accordance with the Fourth Schedule. A listed public company cannot convert into an LLP
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, ss. 55, 56 and 57 with the Second, Third and Fourth Schedules

skeleton.point: Condition for a firm (Second Schedule): the partners of the LLP into which the firm is to be converted must comprise all the partners of the firm and no one else

Conditions for a company (Third and Fourth Schedules): there must be no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of the application, AND the partners of the LLP must comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, Third and Fourth Schedules

skeleton.point: Effect of registration (s. 58): on and from the date of registration there is an LLP by the name specified in the certificate; all tangible and intangible property vested in the firm or company, all assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations and the whole of the undertaking are transferred to and vest in the LLP without further assurance, act or deed; and the firm or company is deemed to be dissolved and its name removed from the register of the Registrar of Firms or the Registrar of Companies

Post-conversion obligations: the LLP must inform the Registrar of Firms or the Registrar of Companies with which the converting entity was registered, about the conversion and the particulars of the LLP, within 15 days of the date of registration; and for twelve months commencing not later than fourteen days after registration every official correspondence must bear a statement that it was converted from a firm or company into an LLP as from the date of registration, together with the name and registration number of the entity converted; pending proceedings, existing agreements, contracts, deeds and employment contracts continue, and approvals, permits and licences transfer subject to the provisions of the Act under which they were issued
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 58(1) and (3), with the Second, Third and Fourth Schedules

questions.topic: Ch 12 · ss. 34, 34A and 35 · Accounts, audit and annual return
questions.stem: Explain the obligations of an LLP relating to books of account, the Statement of Account and Solvency, audit and the annual return, together with the consequences of default. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 34(1): every LLP shall maintain proper books of account relating to its affairs for each year of its existence, on a cash basis or an accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting, at its registered office, for the prescribed period; the books are to be preserved for eight years from the date on which they are made
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 34(1) with Rule 24 of the LLP Rules 2009

skeleton.point: Sections 34(2) and 34(3): within six months from the end of each financial year the LLP shall prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency for that year as at its last day, in the prescribed form, signed by the designated partners; and it shall be filed with the Registrar every year within the prescribed time — Form 8, within 30 days from the end of six months of the financial year to which it relates (that is, by 30 October where the financial year ends on 31 March)
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, ss. 34(2) and 34(3) with Rule 24

skeleton.point: Section 34(4): the accounts of an LLP are to be audited in accordance with the prescribed rules, the Central Government having power to exempt any class of LLPs; Rule 24 exempts an LLP whose turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh in a financial year and whose contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh, so audit becomes compulsory where turnover exceeds ₹40 lakh OR contribution exceeds ₹25 lakh; an exempt LLP may nevertheless get its accounts audited voluntarily

Section 34A: the Central Government may, in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, prescribe standards of accounting and standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, for a class or classes of LLPs
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 34A (inserted by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021)

skeleton.point: Section 35: every LLP shall file an annual return, duly authenticated, with the Registrar within 60 days of the closure of its financial year — Form 11, that is by 30 May where the financial year ends on 31 March
skeleton.citation: LLP Act 2008, s. 35(1) with the LLP Rules 2009

skeleton.point: Consequences of default: penalties on the LLP and on its designated partners under ss. 34(5) and 35(2), adjudicated by an adjudicating officer (the Registrar) under s. 68A with an appeal to the Regional Director within 60 days; a small LLP or start-up LLP pays a reduced penalty; and continued default in filing the Statement of Account and Solvency or the annual return for five consecutive financial years is a ground for winding up by the Tribunal under s. 64(e)

Section 36: the incorporation document, the names of the partners and changes made in them, the Statement of Account and Solvency and the annual return are available for inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee

questions.topic: Ch 12 · Case: converting a firm and a company into an LLP
questions.case: Nandita and Ashwin have carried on a consultancy firm in Pune for eleven years under the Indian Partnership Act 1932. They wish to convert it into an LLP and want their associate Farah, who has never been a partner of the firm, to be a partner of the LLP from the date of conversion. The firm's office premises are mortgaged to a bank. Separately, a client of theirs, Trilochan Systems Private Limited, has four shareholders and a subsisting charge over its receivables, and also wishes to convert into an LLP. In the event, the firm converts without Farah, and the Registrar registers the conversion on 6 July 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP — the three Schedules →

questions.stem: On the facts as originally proposed, the eligibility position of the two converting entities is that:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, ss. 55 and 56 with the Second and Third Schedules

options.text: Both may convert as proposed, since the LLP Act imposes no restriction on who becomes a partner of the converted LLP
options.explanation: Each Schedule imposes an express restriction on the composition of the LLP's partners, and the company Schedules add a security-interest condition.

options.text: The firm cannot convert while Farah is to be a partner of the LLP, because the Second Schedule requires the partners of the LLP to comprise all the partners of the firm and no one else; and Trilochan Systems cannot convert while the charge over its receivables subsists, because the Third Schedule requires that no security interest in its assets be subsisting at the time of the application
options.explanation: Correct. Both defects are eligibility conditions in the respective Schedules, and both can be cured — by admitting Farah after conversion, and by satisfying or releasing the charge before applying.

options.text: The firm cannot convert because its office premises are mortgaged, and Trilochan Systems cannot convert because it has more than two shareholders
options.explanation: The no-security-interest condition applies to company conversions only, so the firm's mortgage is irrelevant; and there is no ceiling on the number of shareholders of a converting company.

options.text: Neither may convert, because only an unlisted public company may convert into an LLP
options.explanation: Sections 55, 56 and 57 permit a firm, a private company and an unlisted public company respectively to convert. Only a LISTED public company is excluded.

questions.stem: On and from the date of registration of the conversion of the firm, the correct position is that:

options.text: All the property, assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations of the firm and the whole of its undertaking are transferred to and vest in the LLP without further assurance, act or deed, and the firm is deemed to be dissolved and removed from the records of the Registrar of Firms
options.explanation: Correct. Section 58(4) effects a statutory vesting and a deemed dissolution; no separate conveyance of the firm's assets is needed.

options.text: The property of the firm vests in the LLP only on execution of separate deeds of conveyance in favour of the LLP
options.explanation: The words 'without further assurance, act or deed' in s. 58(4)(b) are there precisely to avoid separate conveyances.

options.text: The assets of the firm vest in the LLP but its liabilities remain with the erstwhile partners
options.explanation: Liabilities and obligations are expressly included in the vesting. Conversion is not a way of leaving the firm's debts behind.

options.text: The firm continues to exist alongside the LLP until it is separately dissolved by its partners
options.explanation: Section 58(4)(c) deems the firm dissolved and removes it from the records of the Registrar of Firms.

questions.stem: The Registrar registered the conversion of the firm on 6 July 2026. The LLP must inform the Registrar of Firms about the conversion and the particulars of the LLP at the latest by:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 58(1) — 15 days from the date of registration

options.text: 20 July 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one slip. Fifteen days from 6 July 2026 runs to 21 July, not 20 July.

options.text: 5 August 2026
options.explanation: That is 30 days, which is the s. 25(2) period for filing a change in partners, not the s. 58(1) period.

options.text: 21 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 58(1) requires the LLP to inform the Registrar of Firms within 15 days of the date of registration of the conversion.

options.text: 6 October 2026
options.explanation: That is three months, which belongs to s. 17(1) and has nothing to do with conversion.

questions.stem: After the conversion, the LLP's official correspondence must carry a statement about the conversion. The requirement is that:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, Second Schedule — notice of conversion in correspondence

options.text: Every official correspondence must carry the statement permanently, for as long as the LLP exists
options.explanation: The obligation is time-limited to twelve months; it is a transitional warning to those who dealt with the old entity.

options.text: The statement is required only in correspondence with the persons who were creditors of the firm on the date of conversion
options.explanation: The Schedule speaks of every official correspondence, not of a selected class of recipients.

options.text: No such statement is required once the Registrar of Firms has been informed under section 58(1)
options.explanation: The two obligations are separate: intimation to the old Registrar within 15 days, and the correspondence statement for twelve months.

options.text: For twelve months commencing not later than fourteen days after the date of registration, every official correspondence must state that the LLP was, as from the date of registration, converted from a firm into an LLP, and must give the name and registration number of the firm from which it was converted
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs of the requirement, and both time markers — the twelve-month period and the fourteen-day start — come from the Second Schedule.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · Case: designated partners, authority and fraud
questions.case: Meghdoot Infratech LLP has four partners: two individuals, Rahul and Sanya, and two bodies corporate. Rahul and Sanya are the designated partners. During the financial year 2026-27 Rahul stayed in India for 118 days and Sanya for 41 days. During the same year: (i) Sanya, who under the LLP agreement has no authority to place orders above ₹10 lakh, orders ₹35 lakh of steel from a supplier who has never heard of Meghdoot Infratech LLP and believes he is contracting with Sanya's own proprietary business; (ii) Rahul's brother Tarun, who is not a partner, is described as 'Partner - Projects' on the LLP's proposal documents with Rahul's knowledge, and a financier lends ₹60 lakh to the LLP on the faith of Tarun's standing; and (iii) two of the partners deliberately route ₹80 lakh of client advances out of the LLP to defeat its creditors, the other partners knowing nothing of it.

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability — ss. 26 to 31 →

questions.stem: Taking Rahul as the designated partner relied on for the residence requirement of section 7(1), the number of additional days he needed to stay in India during the financial year 2026-27 to satisfy that requirement is:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, Explanation to s. 7 — 120 days during the financial year

options.text: 2 days
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 7 requires a stay of not less than 120 days during the financial year; 120 less the 118 days already spent leaves 2.

options.text: 62 days
options.explanation: That applies a 180-day test, which appears nowhere in the LLP Act.

options.text: 64 days
options.explanation: That applies the pre-2021 test of 182 days during the immediately preceding one year, which the 2021 Amendment replaced.

options.text: Nil — 118 days already satisfies the requirement
options.explanation: 118 days falls two days short of the statutory 120, and the Act allows no rounding.

questions.stem: On item (i), the steel order placed by Sanya:

options.text: Binds the LLP, because Sanya is a partner and every partner is the agent of the LLP under section 26
options.explanation: Section 26 creates the agency, but s. 27(1) then withdraws the LLP's liability where both its limbs are satisfied, as they are here.

options.text: Binds the LLP, because the authority limit is an internal matter in the LLP agreement of which the supplier had no notice
options.explanation: Lack of notice of the limit would help the supplier if he had believed he was dealing with a partner of the LLP. He did not, so limb (b) of s. 27(1) is satisfied against him.

options.text: Does not bind the LLP, because Sanya in fact had no authority to place it and the supplier did not know or believe her to be a partner of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs of s. 27(1) are satisfied — no actual authority, and the third person did not know or believe her to be a partner of the LLP — so the LLP is not bound and the supplier's remedy lies against Sanya.

options.text: Does not bind the LLP, because an order above ₹10 lakh requires the consent of all the partners under the First Schedule
options.explanation: The First Schedule applies only where the LLP agreement is silent, and here the agreement expressly fixes the limit. The First Schedule is not the operative provision.

questions.stem: On item (ii), the position of Tarun and of the LLP in respect of the ₹60 lakh advanced by the financier is that:

options.text: Neither Tarun nor the LLP is liable, because Tarun was never admitted as a partner under section 22
options.explanation: Section 29 fastens liability precisely on a person who is not a partner but is held out as one, and on the LLP that takes the benefit.

options.text: Only the LLP is liable, since the credit was extended to it and Tarun received nothing
options.explanation: Section 29(1) makes the person held out liable to anyone who gave credit on the faith of the representation, whether or not he benefited.

options.text: Only Tarun is liable, since the LLP made no representation of its own
options.explanation: The representation appeared on the LLP's own proposal documents with a designated partner's knowledge, and the proviso to s. 29(1) makes the LLP liable to the extent of the credit received.

options.text: Tarun is liable to the financier under the doctrine of holding out, and the LLP is also liable to the extent of the credit it received or the financial benefit derived from it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 29(1) fixes the person represented to be a partner, and its proviso makes the LLP liable to the extent of the credit received, without prejudice to his liability.

questions.stem: On item (iii), the diversion of ₹80 lakh with intent to defeat creditors means that:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 30(1) and its proviso

options.text: All four partners lose their limited liability, since the LLP is a single legal person
options.explanation: Section 30(1) strips the shield only from the partners who acted with the fraudulent intent. Partners who took no part and knew nothing keep their s. 28(1) protection.

options.text: The liability of the two partners who acted with that intent is unlimited for all or any of the debts and liabilities of the LLP, and the LLP is liable to the same extent unless it establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority
options.explanation: Correct. That is s. 30(1) with its proviso, which puts the burden of proving absence of knowledge or authority on the LLP itself.

options.text: Only the LLP is liable without limit; the partners concerned remain protected by section 28(1)
options.explanation: Section 28(1) protects a partner from liability arising solely by reason of being a partner. It cannot survive a finding of intent to defraud under s. 30.

options.text: No civil consequence follows until the partners concerned are convicted under section 30(2)
options.explanation: The unlimited civil liability under s. 30(1) and the compensation right under s. 30(3) operate independently of, and without waiting for, any criminal proceeding.

questions.topic: Ch 12 · Case: books, audit and the annual filings
questions.case: Chitrakala Designs LLP has a financial year ending 31 March. Its total contribution of partners is ₹27,00,000 and its turnover for the financial year 2027-28 is ₹31,00,000. Its designated partners prepare the Statement of Account and Solvency for the financial year 2027-28 on 12 September 2028 and are working out the filing calendar for that year. They also want to know whether the accounts must be audited and whether the LLP is subject to any prescribed accounting standards.

readLink.label: Read: Books, audit and annual filings — ss. 34, 34A and 35 →

questions.stem: The last date for filing the Statement of Account and Solvency for the financial year 2027-28 with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 34(3) with Rule 24 — 30 days from the end of six months of the financial year

options.explanation: That is the annual-return date under s. 35, which runs 60 days from the closure of the financial year. The two filings run on different clocks.

options.text: 30 October 2028
options.explanation: Correct. Six months from the end of the financial year on 31 March 2028 gives 30 September 2028, and Rule 24 then allows a further 30 days.

options.text: 30 September 2028
options.explanation: That is the end of the six-month period. Rule 24 allows 30 days beyond it for the filing itself.

options.text: 31 October 2028
options.explanation: An off-by-one slip. Thirty days from 30 September 2028 is 30 October, not 31 October.

questions.stem: The last date for filing the annual return of the LLP for the financial year 2027-28 with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 35(1) — 60 days from the closure of the financial year

options.explanation: Correct. Section 35(1) allows 60 days from the closure of the financial year, and 60 days from 31 March 2028 is 30 May 2028.
That reads the period as two calendar months rather than 60 days. Section 35(1) counts days.

options.text: 30 April 2028
options.explanation: That is 30 days, which is the additional period allowed after six months for the Statement of Account and Solvency, not the annual-return period.

options.text: 30 October 2028
options.explanation: That is the Statement of Account and Solvency date under s. 34(3) with Rule 24.

questions.stem: Applying Rule 24 to the LLP's contribution of ₹27,00,000 and its turnover of ₹31,00,000 for the financial year 2027-28, the audit position is that:
questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008, s. 34(4) with Rule 24 — turnover above ₹40 lakh OR contribution above ₹25 lakh

options.text: Audit is not required, because neither figure crosses its threshold
options.explanation: The contribution of ₹27 lakh does cross the ₹25 lakh threshold, so the exemption is lost.

options.text: Audit is required, because the turnover threshold of ₹40 lakh is crossed
options.explanation: The turnover of ₹31 lakh is comfortably below ₹40 lakh. It is the contribution limb that fails.

options.text: Audit is required, because both thresholds are crossed
options.explanation: Only one threshold is crossed. Reading both as breached suggests the two figures have been compared with the wrong limits.

options.text: Audit is required, because the contribution threshold of ₹25 lakh is crossed
options.explanation: Correct. The exemption in Rule 24 is available only where turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh AND contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh, so crossing EITHER limb makes audit compulsory.

questions.stem: On the LLP's remaining queries, the correct position is that:

options.text: The accounting standards notified under section 133 of the Companies Act 2013 apply automatically to every LLP
options.explanation: Section 133 governs companies. For LLPs the power lies in s. 34A of the LLP Act and operates only on notification for a class or classes of LLPs.

options.text: No standards can ever be prescribed for LLPs, and their Statement of Account and Solvency is not open to public inspection
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: s. 34A confers the power, and s. 36 opens the Statement of Account and Solvency to inspection.

options.text: The Central Government may, in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, prescribe standards of accounting and auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for a class or classes of LLPs; and the Statement of Account and Solvency filed by the LLP is available for inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee
options.explanation: Correct. Section 34A names the consultee (NFRA) and the recommending body (ICAI); s. 36 makes the incorporation document, the names of partners and changes in them, the Statement of Account and Solvency and the annual return open to public inspection.

options.text: Standards may be prescribed by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India directly, and the LLP's accounts are confidential to its partners
options.explanation: ICAI recommends; the Central Government prescribes. And s. 36 makes the filed documents public, which is the price of limited liability.
